scenes.headline: 2026 rewrote the record books
scenes.voiceover: In twenty twenty-six, three companies broke into the top three biggest IPOs of all time. And who's number one depends on how you count. An IPO is when a company sells pieces of itself to the public for the first time. Here are the ten biggest ever.

scenes.headline: Researched with help from Claude, an AI made by Anthropic
scenes.body: Anthropic appears in this list. Ranking follows Renaissance Capital's published rule, and every company gets the same treatment.
scenes.voiceover: A quick disclosure: this video was researched with help from Claude, an AI made by Anthropic, which appears in this list. So we use a published ranking rule and give every company the same treatment.

scenes.headline: Money raised when the IPO was priced
scenes.body: Renaissance Capital's rule: not counting extra shares banks may sell later. US dollars at the time, not adjusted for inflation.
scenes.receipt: Renaissance Capital, All Time Largest Global IPOs (base deal size)
scenes.voiceover: The rule: we rank by the money raised when each IPO was priced, as listed by Renaissance Capital. That doesn't count extra shares that banks can sell afterwards, and it's in dollars at the time, not adjusted for inflation. We'll show the extra-share totals too, where they matter.

scenes.headline: Enel
scenes.voiceover: Number ten.

scenes.headline: Italy sells its power company
scenes.voiceover: Enel. It's basically Italy selling shares in its state electricity company, in November nineteen ninety-nine.

scenes.name: Enel
scenes.headline: Enel
scenes.receipt: Renaissance Capital, All Time Largest Global IPOs (base deal size); CNN Money (Nov 1999)
scenes.voiceover: It raised sixteen and a half billion dollars, and a record three point eight million Italians signed up to buy shares. But the first day of trading was weak.

scenes.headline: AIA
scenes.voiceover: Number nine.

scenes.headline: An insurer born from a crisis
scenes.voiceover: AIA, an Asian life insurer. It was spun out of the American insurer AIG, which had to sell assets after the two thousand and eight financial crisis.

scenes.name: AIA
scenes.headline: AIA
scenes.receipt: Renaissance Capital, All Time Largest Global IPOs (base deal size); HKEX statistics (29 Oct 2010)
scenes.voiceover: It raised seventeen point eight billion dollars in Hong Kong in October twenty ten, and set a record for the most shares of one company traded on that exchange's first day.

scenes.headline: Visa
scenes.voiceover: Number eight.

scenes.headline: A payments giant, mid-crisis
scenes.voiceover: Visa, the card payments network. It went public in March two thousand and eight, right in the middle of the financial crisis.

scenes.name: Visa
scenes.headline: Visa
scenes.receipt: Renaissance Capital, All Time Largest Global IPOs (base deal size); vivid.money; ValueWalk
scenes.voiceover: It raised seventeen point nine billion dollars. Priced at forty-four dollars a share, it closed its first day at fifty-six fifty, up about twenty-eight percent.

scenes.headline: NTT DoCoMo
scenes.voiceover: Number seven.

scenes.headline: Japan's mobile phone pioneer
scenes.voiceover: NTT DoCoMo, Japan's biggest mobile network, split off from the national phone company. It listed in Tokyo in October nineteen ninety-eight.

scenes.name: NTT DoCoMo
scenes.headline: NTT DoCoMo
scenes.receipt: Renaissance Capital, All Time Largest Global IPOs (base deal size); Goldman Sachs; The Motley Fool
scenes.voiceover: It raised eighteen point one billion dollars and rose nineteen percent on its first day. In twenty twenty, its parent company NTT took it private again.

scenes.headline: SoftBank Corp
scenes.voiceover: Number six.

scenes.headline: A telecom giant's rough start
scenes.voiceover: SoftBank Corp, the Japanese mobile phone business of the SoftBank group. It listed in Tokyo in December twenty eighteen.

scenes.name: SoftBank Corp
scenes.headline: SoftBank Corp
scenes.receipt: Renaissance Capital, All Time Largest Global IPOs (base deal size); TechCrunch
scenes.voiceover: It raised twenty-one point three billion dollars, but its shares fell fourteen and a half percent on the first day.

scenes.headline: Alibaba
scenes.voiceover: Number five.

scenes.headline: China's online shopping giant
scenes.voiceover: Alibaba, China's online shopping giant. It listed in New York in September twenty fourteen.

scenes.name: Alibaba
scenes.headline: Alibaba
scenes.receipt: Renaissance Capital, All Time Largest Global IPOs (base deal size); Fortune; Bloomberg
scenes.voiceover: It raised twenty-one point eight billion dollars at sixty-eight dollars a share, and jumped thirty-eight percent on day one. With extra shares sold later, the total reached twenty-five billion.

scenes.headline: Saudi Aramco
scenes.voiceover: Number four.

scenes.headline: The world's biggest oil company
scenes.voiceover: Saudi Aramco, the Saudi state oil company. It listed on the Riyadh exchange in December twenty nineteen.

scenes.name: Saudi Aramco
scenes.headline: Saudi Aramco
scenes.receipt: Renaissance Capital, All Time Largest Global IPOs (base deal size); Fortune; Anadolu Agency
scenes.voiceover: It raised twenty-five point six billion dollars and rose ten percent on day one, the most the exchange allows in one day. With extra shares, the total reached twenty-nine point four billion.

scenes.headline: SK hynix
scenes.voiceover: Number three.

scenes.headline: The memory chips behind AI
scenes.voiceover: SK hynix, a South Korean maker of the memory chips used in AI computers. It listed in New York in July twenty twenty-six.

scenes.name: SK hynix
scenes.headline: SK hynix
scenes.receipt: Renaissance Capital, All Time Largest Global IPOs (base deal size); IPOScoop; The Motley Fool
scenes.voiceover: It raised twenty-six point five billion dollars, the biggest US listing ever by a foreign company, and closed its first day up about thirteen percent.

scenes.headline: SpaceX
scenes.voiceover: Number two.

scenes.headline: Rockets, satellites and AI
scenes.voiceover: SpaceX, the rocket and satellite company that also owns the AI firm x A I. It listed in June twenty twenty-six, at one hundred and thirty-five dollars a share.

scenes.name: SpaceX
scenes.headline: SpaceX
scenes.receipt: Renaissance Capital, All Time Largest Global IPOs (base deal size); NPR; Al Jazeera; Dealroom
scenes.voiceover: It raised seventy-five billion dollars and closed day one up nineteen percent. With extra shares sold later, it reached about eighty-six billion, which would make it number one on that measure. It also reported a four point three billion dollar loss in early twenty twenty-six.

scenes.headline: Anthropic
scenes.voiceover: Number one.

scenes.headline: The AI company behind Claude
scenes.receipt: Research assisted by Claude, an AI made by Anthropic, which appears in this list. Ranking follows Renaissance Capital's published rule.
scenes.voiceover: Anthropic, the AI company that makes the Claude assistant. It listed in November twenty twenty-six, selling nine hundred and eighty million shares at eighty-three dollars each.

scenes.name: Anthropic
scenes.headline: Anthropic

stat.label: Nov 2026 · up to ~$93.5bn if option used

scenes.receipt: Renaissance Capital, All Time Largest Global IPOs (base deal size); Anthropic press release (18 Nov 2026); CNBC
scenes.voiceover: It raised eighty-one point three four billion dollars. Its shares opened at one hundred and eleven fifty, but closed the day at ninety-seven seventeen. An option for its banks to sell up to one hundred and forty-seven million more shares is still pending. If fully used, about ninety-three and a half billion.

scenes.eyebrow: Raised at IPO, US$ billions · Renaissance Capital
scenes.headline: Then 2026 happened
scenes.voiceover: Put them side by side, and you can see it. For decades, the record sat between about sixteen and twenty-six billion dollars. Then two companies in twenty twenty-six raised around three times that.

scenes.headline: A first-day jump isn't your gain
scenes.body: Most people can't buy at the IPO price. They buy when trading opens.
scenes.voiceover: One lesson. Most ordinary investors don't get the IPO price. They buy when trading opens. Anyone who bought Anthropic at the one hundred and eleven fifty opening price was about thirteen percent down by the close. A first-day jump isn't your gain.

scenes.headline: OpenAI could be next
scenes.voiceover: And what's next? OpenAI delayed its own IPO, and CNBC reports a plan to list in twenty twenty-seven. This video is education, not investment advice. Which IPO surprised you most? Tell us in the comments.
